To commemorate the occasion, an Iraqi honor guard paraded outside the former palace of Saddam Hussein. Among the primary facilities relinquished during Thursday’s ceremony was the Republican Palace, which had served as the central U.S. headquarters in Baghdad following the 2003 invasion that ousted Iraq's longtime dictator.

"This day is a great day in the history of the Iraqi people," declared Iraqi military spokesman Maj. Gen. Qassim Atta. 

At a joint news conference with Atta, U.S. military spokesman Maj. Gen. David Perkins highlighted the symbolic weight of handing over the historic site: "The palace was handed back to the Iraqi people, significant as a symbol of the head of the government and a sign for increased sovereignty."

Thursday also inaugurated a new U.S.-Iraqi security pact that permits American forces to remain in the country through 2011 under heightened operational restrictions. Similar bilateral agreements have been established with other remaining coalition nations to replace the U.N. mandate that authorized international forces, which expired on Wednesday.

Gen. Perkins clarified that while American troops will continue to operate alongside Iraqi forces, "the Iraqis will be in the lead."

**Title:** A Turning Point in Baghdad: Iraqi Forces Assume Control of the Green Zone

As the clock struck midnight on January 1, 2009, a defining chapter in the modern history of Iraq drew to a close. With the official expiration of the United Nations mandate that had governed international coalition forces since the 2003 invasion, the United States military formally transferred security control of Baghdad’s heavily fortified "Green Zone" to Iraqi forces. This historic transition signaled the end of a foreign military presence operating as an occupying authority and marked a dramatic shift toward restoring complete self-determination to the Iraqi nation.

The foundation for this transfer rested on newly negotiated bilateral pacts, most notably the U.S.-Iraq Security Agreement (also known as the Status of Forces Agreement, or SOFA). Designed to carefully manage the drawdown of coalition personnel while preventing a security vacuum, these pacts established a clear mandate: local troops were to take the primary lead in all security operations, while American forces were restricted to a strictly supporting role. Under the new legal framework, U.S. troops could no longer conduct independent military operations or make arrests without the explicit approval and partnership of the Iraqi judicial system and military command. 

The practical effects of this agreement unfolded swiftly across the four-square-mile International Zone, long considered the nerve center of the foreign presence in Iraq. Iraqi soldiers and police officers immediately assumed sole command of primary security checkpoints, replacing American sentries who had manned the gates for over five years. For the first time in years, entry into the country’s central political district was overseen entirely by Iraqi personnel wearing their national uniform.

Equally significant was the transfer of key physical facilities. Most symbolically, Iraqi forces took control of the iconic Republican Palace. Once the seat of power for Saddam Hussein, the sprawling complex had functioned as the headquarters for the U.S.-led Coalition Provisional Authority and later served as the official American Embassy. During a ceremonial handover, American officials relinquished control of the grand complex, allowing the Iraqi national flag to be raised above the grounds—a powerful visual statement that authority had officially returned to the sovereign state.

For the Iraqi government and its citizens, the successful assumption of security in the capital’s most sensitive zone was a monumental psychological and political milestone. Iraqi Prime Minister Nouri al-Maliki declared the day a national holiday, hailing the shift as a crucial victory for the country's independence and dignity. By demonstrating that domestic security forces were capable of maintaining order over key government infrastructure, the handover established the momentum necessary for the broader, phased withdrawal of foreign troops from Iraqi cities. 

Ultimately, the peaceful transfer of the Green Zone represented far more than a routine change of guard. It stood as a cornerstone in Iraq’s long journey toward re-establishing national sovereignty, serving as a powerful demonstration that the nation was finally equipped to safeguard its own territory, govern its own institutions, and shape its own destiny.

For millions of viewers around the world, the mention of **Baghdad, Iraq**, instantly evokes an iconic image from the history of journalism: a dark, glowing night sky over an ancient city, punctured by the brilliant streaks of anti-aircraft fire. It was January 17, 1991, and **CNN** was making history.

When Operation Desert Storm began, a small team of CNN journalists—including Bernard Shaw, Peter Arnett, and John Holliman—was reporting live from the Al-Rashid Hotel in downtown Baghdad. While other major television networks lost their audio and video feeds, CNN managed to maintain a live four-wire telephone connection. For the first time in human history, the global public listened to a war being broadcast live as it happened. Shaw’s calm, gripping commentary—*"The skies over Baghdad have illuminated"*—didn't just report the news; it redefined it. That night firmly established CNN as a global news powerhouse and marked the birth of the 24-hour real-time news era.

Over the next two decades, the relationship between Baghdad, Iraq, and CNN remained central to international reporting. In 2003, during the U.S.-led invasion of Iraq, CNN correspondents were once again on the front lines, both embedded with military units and reporting from inside the capital. Operating in Baghdad became one of the most dangerous assignments in the world for international journalists, demanding immense courage as reporters navigated bombings, insurgencies, and political volatility to bring the reality of the conflict into living rooms across the globe.

Yet, CNN’s coverage of Baghdad extended beyond military operations. Over the years, the network provided a window into the lived experiences of the Iraqi people. From the tragic toll of civilian casualties and the destruction of cultural heritage to the fragile efforts at democratic elections and economic recovery, CNN’s reporting helped contextualize the deep complexities of post-war Iraq.

Today, Baghdad is a city striving for balance—a vibrant, historic metropolis on the banks of the Tigris River, attempting to move past decades of conflict while navigating complex regional dynamics. As Iraq continues to chart its future, CNN remains a key chronicler of its story. The historic ties between this ancient capital and the pioneer of 24-hour news serve as a lasting testament to the power of broadcast journalism to connect the world to pivotal moments in human history.

counterfactuals.output:
**BAGHDAD (CNN)** — In a historic milestone marking a new chapter for post-invasion Iraq, U.S. military forces officially handed over control of Baghdad’s heavily fortified Green Zone to Iraqi authorities on Thursday.

The transfer of the four-square-mile enclave—the heart of American power in Iraq since the 2003 invasion—serves as a potent symbol of Iraq’s restored sovereignty and a major step toward the eventual withdrawal of U.S. troops.

At a formal ceremony inside the lavish Republican Palace, once Saddam Hussein's seat of power and later the headquarters of the U.S.-led Coalition Provisional Authority, the Iraqi flag was raised as Iraqi security forces formally assumed responsibility for the zone's perimeter and internal checkpoints.

Iraqi Prime Minister Nouri al-Maliki declared the day a national holiday, calling it "Sovereignty Day."

"This palace, which was a symbol of dictatorship, is today returned to the Iraqi people," al-Maliki told a crowd of Iraqi politicians and foreign dignitaries. "Today, all Iraqis regain their dignity, their pride, and their country's complete sovereignty."

### A symbolic fortress changes hands

Formally known as the International Zone, the Green Zone was established shortly after the fall of Baghdad in April 2003. Ringed by massive concrete blast walls, razor wire, and heavily armed U.S. checkpoints, it became an insulated island of relative security amid the chaotic sectarian violence that gripped the rest of the capital, colloquially known to Iraqis as the "Red Zone."

For many Iraqis, the zone was a bittersweet symbol—a sanctuary for foreign diplomats and Iraqi elites that underscored the country's lack of control over its own territory. 

Under the terms of the newly implemented U.S.-Iraq Security Agreement, Iraqi forces now hold primary responsibility for security within the zone. U.S. troops will no longer conduct independent operations in Iraqi cities and will require Iraqi authorization for military actions.

"This is not a sudden departure, but a coordinated and deliberate transition," said a senior U.S. military official speaking on condition of anonymity. "The Iraqi Security Forces have made significant strides over the past two years, and they are ready to step up."

While U.S. forces will remain present inside the zone—transitioning to a new, massive U.S. Embassy compound nearby—their visibility will be drastically reduced. Iraqi soldiers and police officers will now man the primary gates, checking credentials and directing traffic.

### Mixed emotions on Baghdad's streets

Reaction across Baghdad to the handover was a mix of national pride and underlying anxiety. 

For many residents, seeing Iraqi soldiers take full charge of the capital's most secure district was a long-awaited moment. 

"It was embarrassing to see foreign soldiers controlling the heart of our capital," said Ahmed al-Tamimi, a 34-year-old shopkeeper in central Baghdad. "Seeing our own soldiers at the gates makes us feel like Iraq is finally ours again."

However, doubts remain about whether Iraqi forces are fully prepared to maintain security without direct U.S. oversight. While violence in Iraq has dropped dramatically over the past year following the U.S. troop "surge" and the Sunni tribal turn against al-Qaeda in Iraq, insurgent groups continue to carry out devastating sporadic attacks.

Skepticism also lingers over whether the Iraqi government will begin dismantling the giant concrete barriers that divide Baghdad's neighborhoods, a promise made by al-Maliki's administration as part of the normalization process.

### The road ahead

The handover of the Green Zone is the first major deadline under the bilateral security pact ratified late last year. The agreement mandates that all U.S. combat troops must withdraw from Iraqi cities and towns by June 30, with a full exit of all U.S. military forces from the country scheduled by the end of 2011.

For the incoming U.S. administration, the transition in Baghdad aligns closely with plans to shift military focus away from Iraq and toward the escalating conflict in Afghanistan.

U.S. commanders emphasized that while Iraqi forces are now in the lead, American troops remain ready to provide support, including air power, logistics, and intelligence, if requested by the Iraqi government.

"Today is a day of celebration for Iraq," the U.S. military official said. "But the real work—sustaining this security and building a stable nation—is just beginning."

**BAGHDAD** — In a milestone signaling a major shift in the six-year war, the United States military officially transferred control of Baghdad’s heavily fortified International Zone and the iconic Republican Palace to the Iraqi government on Thursday. 

The ceremonial handover, taking place on New Year’s Day, marks a powerful symbol of restored national sovereignty. For years, the 4-square-mile enclave—commonly known as the Green Zone—and the grand, vaulted palace of deposed dictator Saddam Hussein served as the nerve center of the American occupation and the diplomatic seat of Western power in Iraq.

The transition coincides with the official expiration at midnight of the United Nations mandate that had governed the presence of multinational forces in Iraq since the 2003 invasion. Moving forward, the legal basis for the U.S. presence transitions to a newly ratified bilateral security pact, known formally as the Strategic Framework and Status of Forces Agreement (SOFA).

Under the glare of television cameras inside the grand ballroom of the Republican Palace, Iraqi officials celebrated the return of the sprawling estate, which had housed the U.S.-led Coalition Provisional Authority and later the U.S. Embassy, which recently moved into a newly constructed complex nearby.

"This is a historic day for the Iraqi people," said Maj. Gen. Qassim Atta, chief spokesman for the Iraqi military’s Baghdad operations. "Taking back the Republican Palace and the International Zone is a clear, undeniable sign that full sovereignty has returned to our nation. Iraqi forces are fully prepared and ready to step up, take responsibility, and protect our citizens."

U.S. military officials framed the transfer not as an exit, but as the beginning of an equal partnership between two sovereign nations. 

"Today marks the evolution of our relationship with Iraq from a coalition-led security mission to a true strategic partnership," said Maj. Gen. David Perkins, the chief U.S. military spokesman in Iraq. "We are complying fully with the terms of the agreement, working side by side with Iraqi security forces who have shown remarkable progress and dedication in taking the operational lead."

### A New Framework for Security

The expiration of the U.N. mandate removes the legal authority that allowed U.S. forces to conduct unilateral military operations, detain suspects without warrants, and control Iraqi airspace. Under the new security pact negotiated between Washington and Baghdad, the U.S. military must operate under strict new parameters:

*   **Operational Coordination:** All U.S. military operations must now be approved by and coordinated through a joint U.S.-Iraqi committee.
*   **Warrants and Detentions:** American troops can no longer conduct raids or detain Iraqi citizens without a warrant issued by an Iraqi judge, except in cases of active combat operations.
*   **Legal Jurisdiction:** Foreign defense contractors will lose their former immunity under Iraqi law, and U.S. service members could face Iraqi prosecution under specific circumstances for severe crimes committed off-duty and off-base.
*   **Control of Airspace and Borders:** Primary authority over Iraq’s airspace, territorial waters, and international entry points reverts entirely to Iraqi control.

### The Withdrawal Timeline

Central to the security agreement is a strict, binding timeline for the eventual drawdown and total withdrawal of the approximately 140,000 U.S. troops currently stationed in the country.

The pact establishes two major deadlines:
1.  **June 30, 2009:** All U.S. combat troops must withdraw from Iraqi cities, towns, and villages, redeploying to designated bases outside urban centers.
2.  **December 31, 2011:** All U.S. military forces must completely withdraw from Iraq’s land, air, and sea territory. 

While security conditions in Baghdad and across the country have improved dramatically following the 2007–2008 U.S. troop "surge" and a drop in sectarian violence, significant challenges remain. Insurgent groups continue to execute sporadic, lethal bombings, and deep-seated political divisions persist ahead of Iraq's upcoming provincial elections.

Nevertheless, as the Iraqi flag was hoisted above the Republican Palace to replace the American flag, the mood among Iraqi leaders was one of triumph. For the first time since March 2003, the heart of authority in Baghdad is once again entirely in Iraqi hands.

**BAGHDAD — Jan. 1, 2009**

As the dawn fog lifted over the Tigris River on Thursday morning, a quiet revolution took place at the iron-and-concrete gates of Baghdad’s International Zone. 

For nearly six years, American soldiers in heavy body armor were the gatekeepers to the four-square-mile heart of Iraqi power. Today, they stepped back. 

In their place stood Iraqi soldiers, clad in fresh camouflage and wearing black berets, checking badges and searching trunks. Above them, waving in the chilly morning breeze, was the red, white, and black Iraqi flag—recently stripped of the three stars associated with Saddam Hussein’s era, a physical testament to a changing nation.

At midnight, the United Nations mandate authorizing the U.S.-led coalition expired, officially giving way to a new bilateral Security Agreement. With it, the heavily fortified enclave long known as the "Green Zone"—a symbol to many Iraqis of foreign occupation and elite detachment—underwent its most significant transformation since the 2003 invasion.

"Today is a day of restoration," said Prime Minister Nouri al-Maliki in a national address, declaring Jan. 1 a official national holiday dubbed "Sovereignty Day." "This palace, and this country, have been returned to their rightful owners."

The transfer was capped by a solemn ceremony at the majestic, dome-topped Republican Palace, where U.S. officials formally handed control of the iconic complex back to the Iraqi government. For years, the palace served as the nerve center of the American presence in Iraq, housing the U.S. Embassy before its recent move to a newly constructed compound nearby.

At Checkpoint 12, near the shadow of the massive blast walls that encircle the zone, the mood among Iraqi troops was a mixture of fierce pride and quiet anxiety.

"For years, people looked at us and saw the Americans standing behind us," said Capt. Ahmed al-Tamimi, an Iraqi army officer supervising a team of soldiers stopping traffic. "Now, the responsibility is entirely ours. If a car bomb gets through, it is our failure. If Baghdad stays safe, it is our victory."

Under the new terms of the Security Agreement, the roughly 140,000 American troops remaining in Iraq are now subject to strict new limits. They can no longer conduct raids or arrest Iraqi citizens without a warrant from an Iraqi judge, and U.S. forces are slated to withdraw from all Iraqi cities and towns by June 30, with a complete withdrawal scheduled for the end of 2011.

For U.S. forces, the handoff marks the beginning of a delicate transition into a supporting role.

"We aren't leaving overnight, but the dynamic has fundamentally shifted," said Lt. Col. Mark Smith, standing alongside Iraqi commanders near the assassin's gate checkpoint. "We are moving from the front lines to an advisory stance. They are in the driver's seat now."

Yet, outside the concrete ramparts of the International Zone, ordinary Baghdadis greeted the milestone with a mix of hope and skepticism. While violence across the country has dropped significantly from the dark days of the 2006–2007 sectarian slaughter—thanks in part to the U.S. troop "surge" and Sunni tribal uprisings against Al Qaeda—spectacular attacks remain a constant threat. 

In the bustling commercial district of Karrada, where market stalls were filling with morning shoppers, many expressed fear that Iraqi forces, often accused of corruption or sectarian bias, might not be fully prepared to maintain order alone.

"We want the Americans to leave, yes, but we want security more," said Haidar Abdul-Rahman, a 42-year-old shopkeeper, as he swept the pavement outside his store. "If the politicians start fighting each other again, will the Iraqi army protect us, or will they split into militias?"

The true test of Iraq’s new sovereignty will come quickly. Later this month, the country is scheduled to hold provincial elections—a critical milestone that will gauge the stability of Iraq’s fragile political system.

For now, however, the symbolic power of Thursday's transition was undeniable. As an American convoy hummed past an Iraqi-manned checkpoint on the perimeter of the Green Zone this afternoon, the U.S. gunner in the turret raised a hand in salute to an Iraqi soldier standing post. The Iraqi soldier saluted back, adjusted his rifle, and turned to direct the morning traffic into the heart of his capital.

### Iraq takes control of Saddam's former palace in major sovereignty milestone

**January 1, 2009** 
*From CNN Baghdad Bureau Chief Nic Robertson and journalist Qais Al-Bashir*

**(CNN) —** In a deeply symbolic moment marking a dramatic shift in the country's post-war trajectory, American forces on Thursday officially handed control of Saddam Hussein’s former grand presidential palace back to the Iraqi government.

The transfer of the sprawling Republican Palace—a massive, grandly columned complex in the heart of Baghdad’s heavily fortified Green Zone—coincides with the implementation of a landmark bilateral security pact between Washington and Baghdad.

For nearly six years, the grand palace served as the nerve center of the U.S. occupation and subsequent diplomatic presence, functioning as the headquarters for the Coalition Provisional Authority and later as the temporary U.S. Embassy.

On Thursday morning, as the Iraqi national flag was raised above the dome where massive brass busts of the late dictator once stood, Iraqi officials declared the moment a historic victory for self-determination.

"Today, the Iraqi people reclaim what was once stolen by dictatorship and occupied by circumstance," Iraqi Prime Minister Nouri al-Maliki said during a ceremony inside the palace’s opulent, marble-lined ballroom. "This building stands no longer as a monument to tyranny or foreign authority, but as the seat of a fully sovereign, democratic nation. It is a day of national pride and a restoration of our full dignity."

#### Shift in security operations

Under the terms of the new Security Agreement (SOFA) that took effect at midnight, the U.S. military’s mandate under the United Nations expired. American forces must now obtain authorization from Iraqi authorities for combat operations, and Iraqi security forces have taken the primary lead in guarding the capital's International Zone.

U.S. commanders emphasized that while the transfer is highly symbolic, it also reflects a tangible evolution in local military capability.

"This handover is not just a gesture; it represents the growing capacity and readiness of the Iraqi Security Forces," said Maj. Gen. David Perkins, a senior U.S. military spokesman in Baghdad. "They are stepping into the driver's seat of their own national security. Our role is fundamentally changing from leading combat operations to supporting, advising, and enabling our Iraqi partners as they assert operational control across the country."

U.S. personnel had spent the preceding weeks vacating the historic palace, moving diplomatic staff to a newly constructed, purpose-built U.S. Embassy facility located nearby—the largest American diplomatic post in the world.

#### A psychological turning point

For ordinary Iraqis, the return of the palace carries immense psychological weight. Built under King Faisal II and later vastly expanded by Saddam Hussein as a display of power, the site has long been off-limits to the public, first under Saddam's regime and later behind the concrete blast walls of the U.S.-controlled Green Zone.

While severe security challenges remain—including sporadic insurgent attacks and lingering political division—the formal return of the site signals to the world that Iraq's political future is once again in the hands of its own government.

"Saddam ruled from that palace with fear, and the Americans ruled from it with force," said Ahmed al-Tamimi, a 42-year-old shopkeeper in central Baghdad. "To see our own government flag flying up there without foreign troops in charge makes us feel, for the first time in a very long time, that Iraq belongs to Iraqis again."

Iraqi officials stated that the palace will eventually be converted into administrative offices for the Prime Minister and cabinet members, serving as a permanent office of state for Iraq's democratically elected leadership.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a mock news article with the dateline "BAGHDAD, Iraq (CNN) --" explaining the start of the U.S.-Iraqi security pact that set the June 30 city withdrawal deadline and end-of-2011 full departure date.
counterfactuals.output:
**BAGHDAD, Iraq (CNN) --** A landmark security agreement between the United States and Iraq officially took effect Thursday, placing a firm clock on the American military presence and charting a definitive timeline for a total withdrawal of U.S. forces by the end of 2011.

The bilateral accord, officially known as the Status of Forces Agreement (SOFA), establishes two major deadlines that mark the beginning of the end of the U.S.-led military intervention launched in 2003. 

Under the terms of the pact, all U.S. combat troops must withdraw from Iraqi cities, towns, and populated areas by June 30. The final deadline mandates that all remaining American forces depart the country entirely by December 31, 2011, unless a new agreement is negotiated.

Iraqi Prime Minister Nouri al-Maliki hailed the implementation of the pact as a historical victory and a "restoration of full sovereignty." 

In a powerful symbol of the power shift, Iraqi security forces officially took control Thursday of the heavily fortified Green Zone in central Baghdad—the administrative heart of the U.S. occupation—as well as the historic Republican Palace, which had served as the primary U.S. embassy complex.

"This day represents a triumph for all Iraqis," Maliki said in a televised address to the nation. "Iraq is regaining its independence and taking charge of its own destiny."

The pact fundamentally alters how the roughly 140,000 U.S. troops currently deployed in Iraq operate. Effective immediately, American forces are barred from conducting unilateral military raids, searches, or detentions without the explicit authorization and coordination of Iraqi judicial and military authorities. 

Additionally, the agreement ends the broad legal immunity previously granted to American service members and military contractors, opening the door for Iraqi courts to exercise limited jurisdiction over major crimes committed off-duty and off-base.

U.S. commanders emphasized that while the operational rules have changed, the military remains committed to assisting its Iraqi partners.

"We are transitioning from a lead role to a supporting role, but our commitment to a stable, secure, and sovereign Iraq remains firm," said Maj. Gen. David Perkins, a U.S. military spokesman in Baghdad. "We will work side by side with Iraqi security forces as they take the primary responsibility for protecting their citizens."

The agreement's start comes at a crucial political juncture in Washington. President-elect Barack Obama, who made ending the war in Iraq a central promise of his presidential campaign, takes office in less than three weeks. Though negotiated by the outgoing administration of President George W. Bush, the timeline provided by the pact aligns closely with Obama's military objectives.

On the streets of the Iraqi capital, the official handover brought a mixture of optimism and anxiety. 

"We want our sovereignty back, and we want to see the foreign troops leave," said Ahmed al-Tamimi, a shopkeeper in eastern Baghdad. "But the government must prove that our own soldiers can protect us from insurgents without American help."

With the clock now ticking toward the June 30 city withdrawal deadline, U.S. forces are beginning the complex logistical process of shifting bases outside urban centers, clearing the way for Iraqi police and soldiers to take the front line in securing the country's population centers.
